content:
Yesterday we saw the first great truth of Numbers 8:9-11 for the New Creation that we, like the Levites, have been taken from among the people. Not by our own choice or merit, but because Yahweh reached in and called us out. We were redeemed at Calvary, and that redemption means belonging. Today we come to the two remaining acts of that wilderness ceremony: the congregation laying their hands on the Levites, and Aaron presenting them before Yahweh as a wave offering. These two acts raise a searching question for us. The early church laid hands on . But in the Little Flock calling today, we do not practice the laying on of hands in that formal sense. So how does this picture speak to us?

The answer, when we look carefully, is both honest and beautiful.

When all of Israel laid their hands on the Levites, they were not blessing them individually or conferring a spiritual gift. They were doing something communal and weighty: they were transferring their service obligation onto these men. They were saying with their hands what they could not adequately say with words; we are placing you before Yahweh in our place. You will stand where we cannot stand. And the whole congregation had to be present. This was not something a few leaders did quietly. It required the gathered people of Yahweh, all of them, acknowledging together what was happening.

Now consider what baptism is, and what it does in the sight of the congregation. When a believer is baptised, they do not slip into the water in a private corner while no one watches. Baptism is public. The congregation gathers. Everyone is present. And in that moment, something remarkable happens that we do not always think carefully enough about. The believer going down into the water is declaring publicly: I die to what I was. I am buried with Christ. I rise to a new life that belongs entirely to Yahweh (Romans 6:3-4). But the congregation is not merely watching a personal moment. They are witnesses. And witnesses in Scripture are never passive. To witness is to confirm, to receive, to bear responsibility for what was declared before you. When the congregation gathers to witness a baptism, they are; whether they think of it in these terms or not, standing in the place of that old Israel. They are the gathered people of Yahweh, confirming together: this person is being set apart. They are no longer merely one of us in the ordinary sense. They are being presented to Yahweh for His service. We receive them as such. We hold them to it. We carry them before Yahweh in our prayers.

This is why baptism without a congregation is an incomplete picture. From the earliest records in Acts, baptism placed the believer into a body; a gathered people who received them, who would pray for them, who would hold them accountable, and who would themselves be affected by the faithfulness or failure of the one who had just been set apart. The congregation's gathered presence at a baptism is not tradition or ceremony. It is the same instinct that Yahweh built into Numbers 8; the whole people present, hands extended in one mind if not always in form, saying: this one is being presented to Yahweh, and we are witnesses.

In Numbers 8:11, Aaron the high priest was the one who took the Levites and formally presented them before Yahweh as a wave offering.. He brought them forward; into the presence of Yahweh and offered them in presentation.

This was Aaron's unique role as high priest: to stand between the people and Yahweh, and to bring what was being offered into Yahweh's presence so that it could be received.

We have a High Priest. And He is not standing at the entrance of a tent in the Sinai wilderness. He is seated at the right hand of the Father in the heavens, ever living to make intercession for us (Hebrews 7:25). Hebrews 4:14 calls Him our "great High Priest who has passed through the heavens"; not into a room made with human hands, but into the very presence of God Himself. And what does a high priest do? He presents. He brings the offering into God’s sight.

He stands between the worshipper and the Holy One and says: this is what I am bringing before You.

When Christ ascended, He did not ascend empty-handed. He entered the presence of the Father as our Forerunner (Hebrews 6:20); the One who went in ahead of us, on our behalf, to present us. He presented his own blood (Hebrews 9:12) as the sin offering that cleared the way. And He now presents us; the New Creation, before the Father. Just as Aaron lifted the Levites before the Tabernacle and Yahweh said "they are Mine," Christ presents us before the Father and the Father receives us; not because of what we are, but because of who is presenting us and on what basis. "He is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him" (Hebrews 7:25). The presenting is ongoing. Every day. Every moment. Our High Priest has not stopped His work. He is still presenting us before the father.

The most striking detail in Numbers 8:11 is this: the Levites were themselves the wave offering. Not grain. Not an animal. Living men, presented to Yahweh. This is unique in the entire Levitical system; people becoming the offering.

And when Aaron presented them and God received them, they did not go home and resume ordinary life. They became God’s possession permanently.

Their lives, their time, their service; all of it belonged to the One before whom they had been lifted.

Paul uses precisely this language when he writes to the New Creation in Rome: "Present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your reasonable service" (Romans 12:1). A living sacrifice. Not an animal laid on the altar and consumed. A living person; breathing, walking, working, deciding, who has been placed before Yahweh and received as His. The Levites who stood before Aaron on that day were living offerings. They still ate and slept and breathed. But everything they did from that moment forward was done as people who had been presented and received. Their ordinary life was now sacred service.

This is the full picture for the New Creation. We are called out from among the people; redeemed, belonging to Yahweh. We are witnessed into that calling by the gathered congregation at baptism, publicly, communally, with the weight of a people saying together: we receive this one as set apart for God’s service. We are presented before our Father by our High Priest, Christ, who stands in the heavens on our behalf and brings us into the Father's presence continually. And we are received; declared Yahweh's own; living offerings who have not been consumed but set apart. Living, breathing, working, loving, enduring.
But doing all of it as those who have been presented before the Father and received. Nothing we do is secular any more. Nothing is outside the scope of what it means to be Yahweh's. That is the wave offering. That is us.

title: Prayer
text:
O Father, our God,

We are undone when we see what has been done for us and to us.

Taken from among the people. Witnessed by the congregation.

Presented before You by a High Priest who never stops interceding.

And received; declared Yours, as living offerings still walking on the earth.

Forgive us for living as though none of that had happened.

For treating our days as our own and our choices as private.

We are not our own. We were bought. We were set apart. We were presented.

And You said: Mine.

Let that word settle into every corner of our lives;

into how we spend our hours, how we treat the brethren,

how we respond under pressure, what we reach for when no one is watching.

We are Yours. Let us live like it.

O Yahweh, you are my God; I will exalt You, I will praise Your name,

for You have done wonderful things. Isaiah 25:1

We ask this in the name of our great High Priest, our Messiah & our Lord,

who presents us before You and will never let us go.
